blocks.text: **The task.** A sorted array has been rotated at an unknown pivot — `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` might have become `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]`. Find a target value in O(log N), or return −1.
Plain binary search needs a fully sorted array. After rotation, comparing the target to the midpoint no longer tells you which half to search — the array has a discontinuity.
Split a rotated array at any midpoint and **at least one half is still properly sorted**. The discontinuity can only live in one of them.
So: identify the sorted half, check whether the target falls inside its range, and search accordingly.
`nums[low] <= nums[mid]` decides which half is clean. If the left end is not greater than the middle, the left half has no wrap in it.
Inside a sorted half, the target's membership is a simple range check. If it belongs there, search it; if not, the answer must be in the messy half — which will get split again next iteration.

When `low === mid`, a single-element half is trivially sorted, so the comparison must accept equality. Using `<` sends the search down the wrong branch on two-element ranges — a bug that only appears at the very end of a search.
**Time: O(log N)** — the range still halves each step, we just work harder to choose the half.
This is the classic demonstration that binary search needs only a **decidable** halving rule, not literal sortedness.
